notes:
1. Meaning of Consumer Protection

Consumer Protection means safeguarding consumers against:

  • Defective goods.
  • Deficient services.
  • Unfair trade practices.
  • Restrictive trade practices.
  • Misleading advertisements.
  • Unsafe products.
  • Overcharging.
  • Exploitation in digital and traditional markets.

The present principal law is the:

  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
📌 Must-Memorise

Consumer Protection Act → 2019

2. Consumer Protection Forums — Present Terminology

Under the earlier Consumer Protection Act, 1986, the expression:

  • Consumer Forums

was commonly used.

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the statutory bodies are called:

  • Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Older Usage → Consumer Forums

Present Law → Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions

3. Three-Tier Consumer Redressal System

The Consumer Protection Act establishes:

  • District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
  • State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
  • National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
📌 Must-Memorise

District → State → National

4. Meaning of Consumer

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a consumer is generally a person who:

  • Buys goods.
  • Hires services.
  • Avails services

for consideration.

5. Forms of Consideration

Consideration may be:

  • Paid.
  • Promised.
  • Partly paid and partly promised.
  • Payable under deferred-payment arrangements.

6. Transactions Covered

The Act covers transactions through:

  • Offline purchases.
  • Online purchases.
  • Electronic means.
  • Tele-shopping.
  • Direct selling.
  • Multi-level marketing.

7. Who Is Generally Not a Consumer?

A person is generally not treated as a consumer where goods are purchased for:

  • Resale.
  • Commercial purpose.

8. Self-Employment Exception

Goods or services used exclusively for earning livelihood through:

  • Self-employment

may remain within the protection of consumer law according to the statutory framework.

⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Commercial Purpose → Generally Excluded

Self-Employment for Livelihood → Important Exception

9. Six Consumer Rights

The source identifies:

  • Right to Safety.
  • Right to Information.
  • Right to Choose.
  • Right to be Heard.
  • Right to Seek Redressal.
  • Right to Consumer Education.

10. Right to Safety

Consumers have the right to protection against goods and services that may endanger:

  • Life.
  • Health.
  • Property.

11. Right to Information

Consumers have the right to accurate information about matters such as:

  • Quality.
  • Quantity.
  • Price.
  • Purity.
  • Standard.
  • Composition.
  • Potency.

12. Right to Choose

Consumers should have:

  • Access to alternatives.
  • Freedom to choose among available goods and services.

13. Right to be Heard

Consumers have the right to:

  • Present complaints.
  • Raise grievances.
  • Have their concerns considered by appropriate authorities.

14. Right to Seek Redressal

Consumers may seek remedies against:

  • Defective goods.
  • Deficient services.
  • Unfair trade practices.
  • Restrictive trade practices.
  • Other violations covered by consumer law.

15. Right to Consumer Education

Consumers have the right to awareness regarding:

  • Their rights.
  • Their responsibilities.
  • Available remedies.
  • Complaint procedures.

16. Consumer Protection Act, 1986

The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was India's earlier comprehensive consumer-protection legislation.

It introduced:

  • Consumer rights.
  • Consumer forums.
  • Three-tier consumer dispute redressal.

17. Consumer Protection Act, 2019

The 2019 Act:

  • Replaced the 1986 Act.
  • Modernised India's consumer-protection framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

1986 Act → Replaced by 2019 Act

18. Major Innovations of 2019 Act

The source highlights:

  • Central Consumer Protection Authority.
  • Product liability.
  • Consumer mediation.
  • Regulation of misleading advertisements.
  • E-commerce protection.
  • Strengthened Consumer Commissions.

19. CCPA

CCPA stands for:

  • Central Consumer Protection Authority.

20. Legal Basis of CCPA

CCPA is established under:

  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

21. Nature of CCPA

CCPA is primarily a:

  • Central regulatory authority

for protection of:

  • Consumer rights.
  • Consumers as a class.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CCPA → Regulatory Authority

Consumer Commission → Dispute Redressal Authority

22. Purpose of CCPA

The CCPA seeks to:

  • Protect consumer rights.
  • Prevent unfair trade practices.
  • Regulate misleading advertisements.
  • Promote consumer welfare.
  • Protect consumers collectively.

23. Composition of CCPA

The source states that CCPA consists of:

  • Chief Commissioner.
  • Other Commissioners.

24. Appointment

CCPA Commissioners are appointed by:

  • Central Government

according to the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

25. Investigation Wing

CCPA has an:

  • Investigation Wing

headed by:

  • Director-General.
📌 Must-Memorise

CCPA Investigation Wing → Director-General

26. Powers of CCPA

CCPA may:

  • Conduct inquiries.
  • Order investigations.
  • Recall unsafe goods.
  • Withdraw hazardous services.
  • Direct reimbursement of price.
  • Stop unfair trade practices.
  • Stop misleading advertisements.
  • Impose penalties according to law.

27. Misleading Advertisements

CCPA may act against:

  • False advertisements.
  • Misleading claims.
  • Misrepresentation.
  • False promotional promises.

28. Endorsements

Persons endorsing products are expected to exercise:

  • Due diligence.

Action may be taken against endorsers where statutory conditions are satisfied.

29. District Commission

The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission functions at:

  • District level.

30. Position in Hierarchy

It is the:

  • First level

of the three-tier consumer dispute redressal hierarchy.

31. Composition

District Commission consists of:

  • President.
  • Members

appointed according to the Act and applicable rules.

32. Functions of District Commission

It may:

  • Receive complaints.
  • Conduct hearings.
  • Examine evidence.
  • Decide consumer disputes.
  • Grant statutory relief.

33. State Commission

The State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission functions at:

  • State level.

34. Composition

State Commission consists of:

  • President.
  • Members

appointed according to the Act and applicable rules.

35. Functions of State Commission

The State Commission:

  • Exercises original jurisdiction under the Act.
  • Hears appeals against District Commission orders.
  • Exercises revisional jurisdiction in specified cases.
📌 Must-Memorise

District Appeal → State Commission

36. NCDRC

NCDRC stands for:

  • National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.

37. Position

NCDRC functions at:

  • National level.

It is the highest Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Act.

38. Composition

NCDRC consists of:

  • President.
  • Members

appointed according to the Consumer Protection Act and applicable rules.

39. Functions of NCDRC

NCDRC:

  • Exercises original jurisdiction.
  • Hears appeals from State Commissions.
  • Exercises revisional jurisdiction under the Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Appeal → National Commission

40. Appeal from NCDRC

Appeals from specified NCDRC orders lie to:

  • Supreme Court of India

in accordance with the Consumer Protection Act.

📌 Must-Memorise

District → State → National → Supreme Court

41. Meaning of Jurisdiction

Jurisdiction means:

  • Legal authority of a Consumer Commission to hear and decide a dispute.

42. Types of Jurisdiction

The source identifies:

  • Territorial Jurisdiction.
  • Pecuniary Jurisdiction.
  • Original Jurisdiction.
  • Appellate Jurisdiction.
  • Revisional Jurisdiction.

43. Territorial Jurisdiction

Territorial jurisdiction determines:

  • Geographical area in which a complaint may be filed.

44. Pecuniary Jurisdiction

Pecuniary jurisdiction is based upon:

  • Value of goods or services paid as consideration.

45. Pecuniary Limits

The source specifically notes that:

  • Pecuniary limits are prescribed under the Act and relevant rules.
  • They may be revised by Central Government notification.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Do not treat old pecuniary limits as permanently fixed.

The source deliberately avoids fixed figures because they can be revised.

46. Original Jurisdiction

Original Jurisdiction means:

  • Hearing and deciding a complaint in the first instance.

47. Appellate Jurisdiction

Appellate Jurisdiction means:

  • Hearing an appeal against an order of a lower Consumer Commission.

48. Revisional Jurisdiction

Revisional Jurisdiction enables State and National Commissions to examine specified subordinate orders for:

  • Legality.
  • Propriety.
  • Jurisdictional correctness.

49. Consumer

A complaint may be filed by:

  • A consumer.

50. Consumer Association

A complaint may be filed by:

  • Recognised Consumer Association.

51. Consumers with Same Interest

A complaint may be filed by:

  • One or more consumers having the same interest.

52. Governments

A complaint may also be filed by:

  • Central Government.
  • State Government.

53. CCPA

The source identifies:

  • Central Consumer Protection Authority

as another complainant where authorised under the Act.

54. Legal Heir

Where a consumer has died, a complaint may be brought by:

  • Legal heir.
  • Legal representative.

55. Defective Goods

A complaint may arise where goods contain:

  • Defect.

56. Defect

Defect means a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in matters such as:

  • Quality.
  • Quantity.
  • Potency.
  • Purity.
  • Standard.
📌 Must-Memorise

Defect → Goods

57. Deficiency

Deficiency means a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in:

  • Quality.
  • Nature.
  • Manner of performance

of a service.

📌 Must-Memorise

Deficiency → Services

58. Examples of Deficient Services

The source identifies examples such as:

  • Banking.
  • Insurance.
  • Transport.
  • Healthcare subject to applicable law.
  • Housing services.

59. Unfair Trade Practice

A complaint may arise from:

  • Unfair Trade Practice.

60. Examples of Unfair Trade Practices

Examples include:

  • False representation.
  • Misleading advertisements.
  • Fake discounts.
  • False quality claims.
  • False guarantees.
  • Counterfeit goods.
  • Hidden charges.
  • Non-issuance of bills.

61. Restrictive Trade Practice

A Restrictive Trade Practice may:

  • Manipulate price.
  • Manipulate delivery conditions.
  • Delay supply.
  • Force purchase of unwanted goods.
  • Restrict consumer choice.

62. Overcharging

A consumer may complain where:

  • Excess price is charged contrary to applicable legal or contractual standards.

63. Hazardous Goods

Complaints may arise from sale of:

  • Hazardous.
  • Unsafe

goods or services.

64. Misleading Advertisement

A misleading advertisement may:

  • Give false information.
  • Conceal material facts.
  • Make false promises.
  • Exaggerate product performance.
  • Mislead purchasing decisions.

65. Product Liability

Consumers may file complaints relating to:

  • Product Liability

where conditions under the Consumer Protection Act are satisfied.

66. Mode of Filing

A complaint may be filed:

  • Physically.
  • Electronically

according to prescribed procedure.

67. Basic Contents

A complaint should ordinarily include:

  • Name and address of parties.
  • Facts.
  • Nature of grievance.
  • Relief sought.
  • Supporting documents.

68. Important Supporting Documents

Useful documents include:

  • Bills.
  • Receipts.
  • Tax invoices.
  • Warranty cards.
  • Correspondence.
  • Photographs.
  • Expert reports.
  • Other relevant evidence.

69. Procedure after Filing

The Consumer Commission generally:

  • Examines complaint.
  • Issues notice.
  • Receives opposite party's response.
  • Examines evidence.
  • Conducts hearing.
  • Passes order.

70. Nature of Proceedings

Consumer proceedings are designed to be:

  • Simple.
  • Speedy.
  • Consumer-friendly.
  • Affordable.
  • Less formal than ordinary civil litigation.

71. Removal of Defect

The Commission may order:

  • Removal of defects in goods.

72. Replacement

It may direct:

  • Replacement of defective goods.

73. Refund

It may order:

  • Refund of consideration or price according to law.

74. Compensation

The Commission may award:

  • Compensation for loss or injury

where statutory conditions are satisfied.

75. Unfair Trade Practice

The Commission may direct:

  • Discontinuance of unfair trade practices.

76. Hazardous Goods

Relief may include:

  • Withdrawal of hazardous goods.

77. Misleading Advertisements

Orders relating to:

  • Discontinuance of misleading advertisements

may be made where authorised by the Act.

78. Litigation Costs

Consumer Commissions may award:

  • Costs of litigation.

79. Appellate Hierarchy

The appellate chain is:

  • District Commission → State Commission.
  • State Commission → National Commission.
  • National Commission → Supreme Court.

80. Limitation for Appeals

Appeals must be filed:

  • Within the period prescribed under the Act.
  • Delay may be condoned where legally permissible.

81. Consumer Mediation

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduced:

  • Consumer Mediation

as an Alternative Dispute Resolution mechanism.

📌 Must-Memorise

2019 Act → Statutory Consumer Mediation

82. Purpose of Mediation

Mediation seeks to:

  • Resolve disputes amicably.
  • Reduce litigation.
  • Save time.
  • Reduce costs.
  • Promote mutually acceptable settlement.

83. Consumer Mediation Cells

Consumer Mediation Cells are established to facilitate:

  • Mediation of disputes referred by Consumer Commissions.

84. Advantages of Mediation

Benefits include:

  • Faster settlement.
  • Lower cost.
  • Flexible procedure.
  • Voluntary agreement.
  • Reduced caseload.
  • Better satisfaction.

85. Mediation vs Consumer Commission

Mediation:

  • Amicable settlement.
  • Based on mutual agreement.
  • Flexible.

Consumer Commission:

  • Formal adjudication.
  • Gives binding order under Act.

86. Meaning

Product Liability means legal responsibility to compensate for harm caused by:

  • Defective product.
  • Deficient product-related service.

87. Major Innovation

The attachment identifies Product Liability as:

  • One of the major innovations of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

88. Persons against Whom Action May Be Brought

Product Liability Action may be brought against:

  • Product manufacturer.
  • Product seller.
  • Product service provider

where statutory conditions are satisfied.

89. Grounds of Product Liability

The source lists:

  • Manufacturing defect.
  • Design defect.
  • Defective product.
  • Deficient service.
  • Inadequate instructions.
  • Inadequate warnings.

90. Product Liability vs Defect

Defect:

  • Fault in goods.

Product Liability:

  • Legal responsibility for harm resulting from product-related defects or deficiencies.

91. Meaning of E-Commerce

E-Commerce means buying and selling through:

  • Electronic.
  • Digital

platforms.

92. Examples

Examples include:

  • Online marketplaces.
  • Shopping websites.
  • Mobile applications.
  • Digital platforms.

93. E-Commerce under Consumer Law

Online consumers are protected by:

  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
  • Rules framed under the Act.

94. Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules

The source specifically identifies:

  • Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.
📌 Must-Memorise

E-Commerce Rules → 2020

95. E-Commerce Obligations

E-commerce entities are subject to requirements relating to:

  • Transparency.
  • Consumer grievance mechanisms.
  • Disclosure of information.
  • Fair business practices.

96. Common Online Consumer Complaints

Consumers may complain about:

  • Defective goods.
  • Delayed delivery.
  • Refund problems.
  • Deficient services.
  • Misleading advertisements.
  • Unfair trade practices.

97. Digital Consumer Risks

The source identifies:

  • Fake websites.
  • Identity theft.
  • Payment fraud.
  • Counterfeit products.
  • Cyber scams.
  • Fake reviews.
  • Manipulated ratings.
  • False product claims.

98. Responsible Consumer Behaviour

Consumers should:

  • Verify quality.
  • Read labels.
  • Check expiry dates.
  • Preserve bills and invoices.
  • Follow instructions.
  • Report unfair practices.
  • Avoid misuse of consumer rights.
  • Make informed purchases.

99. Consumer Awareness

Consumer awareness means knowledge of:

  • Rights.
  • Responsibilities.
  • Product information.
  • Legal remedies.
  • Complaint procedures.

100. Consumer Organisations

Consumer organisations help through:

  • Consumer education.
  • Awareness.
  • Legal assistance.
  • Advocacy.
  • Public campaigns.

101. No Separate Fundamental Right

The Constitution does not expressly create a separate:

  • Fundamental Right to Consumer Protection.

Consumer protection is supported by several constitutional provisions and welfare principles.

102. Article 14

Article 14 guarantees:

  • Equality Before Law.
  • Equal Protection of Laws.

Consumer laws must operate:

  • Fairly.
  • Without arbitrary discrimination.

103. Article 19(1)(g)

Article 19(1)(g) guarantees freedom to:

  • Practise a profession.
  • Carry on occupation.
  • Carry on trade.
  • Carry on business.

104. Reasonable Restrictions

Business freedom under Article 19(1)(g) is subject to:

  • Reasonable restrictions in public interest.

Consumer-protection regulations are connected with this constitutional principle.

105. Article 21

Article 21 protects:

  • Life.
  • Personal Liberty.

Unsafe goods and hazardous services can affect:

  • Health.
  • Safety.
  • Life.

106. Article 38

Article 38 directs the State to promote:

  • Social order.
  • Social justice.
  • Welfare of people.
  • Reduction of inequalities.

107. Article 39(b)

Article 39(b) directs that material resources should be distributed to:

  • Best serve the Common Good.

108. Article 39(c)

Article 39(c) seeks to prevent:

  • Concentration of wealth

to the common detriment.

109. Article 39(e)

Article 39(e) directs protection of:

  • Health.
  • Strength

of citizens.

110. Article 47

Article 47 directs improvement of:

  • Nutrition.
  • Standard of living.
  • Public health.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 47 → Nutrition + Standard of Living + Public Health

111. Article 48A

Article 48A directs the State to:

  • Protect.
  • Improve

the environment.

112. Article 51A(g)

Article 51A(g) places a Fundamental Duty on citizens to:

  • Protect and improve the natural environment.

113. Article 51A(j)

Article 51A(j) requires citizens to:

  • Strive towards excellence

in individual and collective activity.

114. Article 246

Article 246 deals with:

  • Distribution of legislative powers between Parliament and State Legislatures.

115. Seventh Schedule

Consumer-related legislation may involve subjects distributed across:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List

depending on the subject matter.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is:

  • Central Parliamentary legislation.

116. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, 1994

The Supreme Court held that:

  • Housing construction and related services of statutory development authorities may constitute “service” under consumer law.
📌 Must-Memorise

LDA v M.K. Gupta → 1994 → Housing Service + Government Authority Liability

117. Importance of M.K. Gupta Case

Consumers may seek compensation for:

  • Deficiency.
  • Delay.
  • Negligence

by public development authorities where consumer law applies.

118. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, 1995

The Supreme Court held:

  • Medical services rendered for consideration generally fall within “service” under consumer law.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMA v V.P. Shantha → 1995 → Medical Services

119. Completely Free Medical Services

The source states that services rendered:

  • Completely free of charge

are generally outside the consumer-law framework discussed in the judgment.

120. LIC v. Consumer Education & Research Centre, 1995

The Supreme Court emphasised protection of:

  • Consumer interests

in insurance-related matters according to law.

121. Bharathi Knitting Company v. DHL, 1996

The Supreme Court held:

  • Valid contractual terms are ordinarily binding on parties

subject to applicable law.

122. Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia, 1998

The Court awarded compensation for:

  • Medical negligence.

The source notes that both:

  • Patient.
  • Parents

may claim compensation depending upon circumstances.

123. Charan Singh v. Healing Touch Hospital, 2000

The Supreme Court held compensation should be:

  • Fair.
  • Reasonable.
  • Just.

It should be neither:

  • Excessive.
  • Inadequate.

124. Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, 2004

The Supreme Court clarified that compensation in housing disputes depends upon:

  • Facts.
  • Nature of deficiency.
  • Actual loss.

Compensation cannot be:

  • Arbitrary.

125. National Seeds Corporation v. M. Madhusudhan Reddy, 2012

The Supreme Court held that farmers purchasing seeds for cultivation may maintain consumer complaints:

  • Where statutory requirements are satisfied.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Seeds Corporation → 2012 → Farmers as Consumers

126. Defective Seeds

The judgment strengthened consumer remedies where:

  • Defective seeds caused crop loss.

127. Pioneer Urban Land v. Govindan Raghavan, 2019

The Supreme Court held that:

  • One-sided.
  • Unreasonable

contractual clauses cannot automatically bind consumers merely because they appear in a standard-form builder agreement.

📌 Must-Memorise

Pioneer Urban → 2019 → Unfair Builder-Buyer Terms

128. Judicial Principles

The attachment identifies principles including:

  • Consumer law should receive consumer-friendly interpretation.
  • Deficiency in service gives rise to remedies.
  • Government agencies may be liable where they provide deficient services.
  • Medical services for consideration generally fall within consumer law.
  • Compensation must be fair and reasonable.
  • Farmers may qualify as consumers in appropriate cases.
  • Unfair contractual terms may be judicially scrutinised.

129. CCPA vs Consumer Commission

CCPA:

  • Regulatory authority.
  • Protects consumers as a class.
  • Investigates unfair trade practices.
  • Regulates misleading advertisements.

Consumer Commission:

  • Quasi-judicial dispute-redressal body.
  • Decides consumer complaints.
  • Grants individual relief.

130. CCPA vs NCDRC

CCPA:

  • Regulatory and administrative role.
  • Investigates consumer-right violations.

NCDRC:

  • Highest Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
  • Hears complaints and appeals.

131. Defect vs Deficiency

Defect:

  • Goods.

Deficiency:

  • Services.

132. Unfair vs Restrictive Trade Practice

Unfair Trade Practice:

  • Deception.
  • False claims.
  • Misleading practices.

Restrictive Trade Practice:

  • Restricts consumer choice.
  • Manipulates supply or purchase conditions.

133. Original vs Appellate Jurisdiction

Original:

  • Complaint heard for first time.

Appellate:

  • Appeal against lower Commission's decision.

134. Territorial vs Pecuniary Jurisdiction

Territorial:

  • Geographical competence.

Pecuniary:

  • Financial competence based on consideration under applicable law and rules.

135. Consumer Awareness vs Consumer Protection

Consumer Awareness:

  • Knowledge of rights and remedies.

Consumer Protection:

  • Legal and institutional enforcement of those rights.

What is a defect? → Fault or shortcoming in goods.

What is deficiency? → Fault or inadequacy in service.

Defect relates to what? → Goods.

Deficiency relates to what? → Services.

What is Unfair Trade Practice? → Deceptive or unfair method used to promote sale or supply.

Give examples. → False claims, misleading advertisements, fake discounts, counterfeit products and hidden charges.

What is Restrictive Trade Practice? → Practice manipulating supply, price or purchase conditions in a manner restricting consumers.

What is Territorial Jurisdiction? → Geographical authority of a Commission.

What is Pecuniary Jurisdiction? → Financial authority based on value of consideration under applicable law and rules.

Should fixed old pecuniary limits be permanently memorised from this attachment? → No; the source notes they may be revised by Central Government notification.

What is Original Jurisdiction? → Power to hear a complaint in the first instance.

What is Appellate Jurisdiction? → Power to hear an appeal from a lower Commission.

What is Revisional Jurisdiction? → Power to examine specified subordinate orders for legality or propriety.

Who may file a consumer complaint? → Consumer, recognised Consumer Association, consumers with same interest, Central Government, State Government, CCPA where authorised, or legal heir/legal representative.

Can a complaint be filed electronically? → Yes.

What documents are useful? → Bills, receipts, invoices, warranty cards, correspondence, photographs and expert reports.

What remedies can a Consumer Commission grant? → Removal of defect, replacement, refund, compensation, discontinuance of unfair practices, withdrawal of hazardous goods and litigation costs.

What is Consumer Mediation? → Alternative mechanism for amicable settlement of consumer disputes.

Which Act introduced the statutory mediation framework? → Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

What are advantages of mediation? → Faster, cheaper, flexible and mutually acceptable settlement.

What is Product Liability? → Legal responsibility to compensate for harm caused by defective products or deficient related services.

Against whom may Product Liability Action be brought? → Manufacturer, product seller or product service provider where statutory conditions apply.

Give grounds for product liability. → Manufacturing defect, design defect, deficient service, inadequate instructions or warnings.

Does the 2019 Act cover e-commerce? → Yes.

Which rules are specifically mentioned for e-commerce? → Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.

What obligations apply to e-commerce entities? → Transparency, grievance mechanisms, disclosure and fair business practices.

Does Constitution provide a separate Fundamental Right to Consumer Protection? → No.

Which Article provides Equality Before Law? → Article 14.

Which Article protects freedom of business subject to reasonable restrictions? → Article 19(1)(g).

Which Article protects life and personal liberty and is relevant to unsafe goods? → Article 21.

Which Article directs promotion of social welfare? → Article 38.

Which Article concerns distribution of material resources for Common Good? → Article 39(b).

Which Article seeks to prevent concentration of wealth? → Article 39(c).

Which Article directs improvement of public health? → Article 47.

Which Article concerns environmental protection by the State? → Article 48A.

Which Fundamental Duty concerns the environment? → Article 51A(g).

Which Article distributes legislative powers? → Article 246.

Which landmark case brought housing services of statutory authorities within consumer law? → Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, 1994.

Which case held medical services for consideration generally constitute service? → Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, 1995.

Which case dealt with medical-negligence compensation to child and parents? → Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia, 1998.

Which case said compensation must be fair, reasonable and just? → Charan Singh v. Healing Touch Hospital, 2000.

Which case dealt with compensation for delayed housing services? → Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, 2004.

Which case strengthened farmers' consumer rights concerning defective seeds? → National Seeds Corporation v. M. Madhusudhan Reddy, 2012.

Which case protected homebuyers against one-sided builder agreements? → Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan, 2019.

What is the easiest chapter memory line? → Consumer Protection Act, 2019 created a modern three-tier redressal system—District, State and National Commissions—supported by CCPA regulation, mediation, product liability and protection for e-commerce consumers.
